CausalChain: Hypoxia in tumor microenvironment -> Enhanced autophagy in CAFs -> Increased IL-6 secretion from CAFs -> IL-6 binds to receptors on tumor cells -> Activation of JAK2 -> Phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT3 -> Upregulation of EMT and chemoresistance genes -> Increased tumor invasion and therapy resistance
Hypothesis: Under hypoxic conditions, autophagy in cancer-associated fibroblasts drives IL-6 overproduction, which activates the JAK2/STAT3 pathway in neighboring tumor cells, promoting EMT and chemoresistance; thus, inhibition of CAF autophagy may reduce IL-6–mediated tumor aggressiveness and enhance treatment response.
Abstract: We propose that in hypoxic tumor microenvironments, cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs) undergo enhanced autophagy, which in turn elevates their secretion of IL‐6. This increased IL‐6 production acts in a paracrine manner on nearby tumor cells to activate the JAK2/STAT3 signaling cascade, culminating in the transcription of genes that promote epithelial‐mesenchymal transition (EMT), metastatic traits, and chemoresistance. By targeting the autophagic machinery in CAFs, it may be possible to dampen IL‐6 secretion and thereby attenuate the oncogenic IL‐6/JAK2/STAT3 axis, presenting a novel strategy for intervention in several solid tumors.
